# Results {#reses-peses}

## Population growth rates ($\lambda$)

The median population growth rate when excluding the effects of fishing ($\lambda_{dem}$) for the 77 stocks in this analysis was `r med.lambda.F0`, representing an innate capacity for annual population growth of approximately `r med.r.F0`%. Aggregating over years, the stock with highest median theoretical population growth rate was Atlantic cod in the Irish Sea (median $\lambda_{dem}$ = `r max.median.lam.nf`) and the lowest was pollock in the Gulf of Alaska (median $\lambda_{dem}$ = `r min.median.lam.nf`; Table \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas)).  When the effects of fishing were accounted for, the overall median population growth rate ($\lambda_{real}$) dropped to `r med.lambda.F`, which corresponds to overfishing by  `r -med.r.F`% annually (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). 

The realized range of population growth rates was much narrower and the median $\lambda_{real}$ was below 1 more than 50% of the time in `r prop.usually.lt.1.fish`% of the stocks (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). However, many of the stocks included in our analysis experienced infrequent large recruitment events that resulted in high $\lambda_{real}$ estimates (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). For example, while the Gulf of Alaska pollock stock had the lowest median $\lambda_{dem}$ (`r min.median.lam.nf`), it had a mean $\lambda_{dem}$ of `r mean.nf.of.min.median.lam.nf`, and when the effects of fishing were included, this stock had the $8^{th}$ highest mean $\lambda_{real}$ (`r mean.fish.of.min.median.lam.nf`, Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). 

Mean $\lambda_{real}$ was lower than the median for just `r n.stocks-n.mn.higher.med.fish` of the `r n.stocks` stocks, and the mean $\lambda_{real}$ was less than one for `r num.mn.lambda.fish.lt.1` of the `r n.stocks` stocks, indicating that years of high population growth resulted in a net positive productivity for most stocks. The majority of the stocks with a mean $\lambda_{real}$ value less than one were in the central or NW Atlantic (N = `r n.mn.lt.1.nw.ice`), and included `r n.cod.low.mn`  of the `r n.cod` Atlantic cod (*G. morhua*) stocks.

Several species are harvested throughout the North Atlantic, including two relatively large and long-lived Gadidae species: Haddock (*Melanogrammus aeglefinus*) and Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*). These two species exhibited some of the highest variability in population growth rates both over time and among stocks (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig)). For both of these species, the variability in the population growth rate declined moving from the Eastern Atlantic to the Western Atlantic (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-sd-fig)). The pattern was most pronounced for Atlantic cod, where stocks in the Eastern Atlantic rarely experienced high values of $\lambda$ (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-sd-fig)). Pollock (*Pollachius virens*) is another Gadidae species harvested across the North Atlantic. The variability in $\lambda$ was lower for this species throughout its range (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-sd-fig)). Atlantic herring (*Clupea harengus*) is a relatively small fast growing species also found throughout the North Atlantic. However, there were no clear regional patterns in $\lambda$ for this species and its variability in $\lambda$ was lower than observed in several Atlantic cod and haddock stocks.  

Two relatively short-lived and fast-growing species, (Sand eel [*Ammodytes tobianus*] and Norway pout [*Trisopterus esmarkii*]) in the North Sea exhibited high variability in $\lambda$, though this variability was smaller than that observed in the haddock and Atlantic cod stocks in the area (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). For the remainder of other stocks in this analysis, years in which the value of $\lambda_{dem}$ were elevated (e.g., above $\approx$ 1.5) were rarer, but no clear taxonomic or regional patterns were evident, with whiting (*Merlangus merlangus*) in the Celtic Sea, summer flounder (*Paralichthys dentatus*) and scup (*Stenotomus Chrysops*) in the Western Atlantic, and  Gulf of Alaska pollock (*Gadus chalcogrammus*) all having moderate variability in $\lambda$ (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)).

There was no clear temporal trend in the lambda estimates, however $\lambda_{dem}$ in the 2000s was low (`r med.lam.nf.2000s`), and in the 2010s the standard deviation of $\lambda_{dem}$ was higher than in the other decades, resulting in a low median $\lambda_{dem}$ (`r med.lam.nf.2010s`), but a mean $\lambda_{dem}$ estimate similar to what was observed before the 2000s (`r mean.lam.nf.2010s`; Table \@ref(tab:tab-lamda-temp)). The high standard deviation in the 2010s was somewhat impacted by a single stock (CS RA *M. aeglefinus*). When this stock was removed from the analysis, the standard deviation remained the highest in the time series, but was not as extreme (sd of $\lambda_{dem}$ declined to `r sd.lam.nf.2010s.no.had`), while the median and mean $\lambda$'s remained similar to values observed before the 2000s (e.g., the median and mean $\lambda_{dem}$ were `r med.lam.nf.2010s.no.had` and `r mean.lam.nf.2010s.no.had` respectively). This analysis also indicated that relative abundances (proportion of maximum observed) of the stocks have been in decline over the last 40 years, with the lowest values observed in the 2010s (Table \@ref(tab:tab-lamda-temp)).

## Density Dependence

Overall both $\lambda_{dem}$ and $\lambda_{real}$ increased as abundance declined.  The changes in the rate of population growth were more pronounced at low and high abundance levels. The relationship between $\lambda$ and the proportion of maximum abundance was relatively flat when abundance ranged between 40-70% of maximum (Figure \@ref(fig:dd-overall-plt)). The $\lambda_{dem}$ remained above one when stocks approached their maximum observed abundance in more than `r pa.lam.nf.at.one`% of the stocks (Tables \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas) and \@ref(tab:tab-lamda-diffs) and Figures A1 and A2). However, $\lambda_{real}$ dropped below one when the stock abundance exceeded approximately `r pa.lam.fish.at.one`% of the maximum abundance. At lower abundances, the model estimated $\lambda_{dem}$ increased as abundance declined more slowly than $\lambda_{real}$ (Figure \@ref(fig:dd-overall-plt)). This is likely due to reductions in fishing mortality at low abundance, but since the fitted values did not overlap, some fishing mortality remained even at very low abundance. For the vast majority of stocks the lowest model-estimated values of $\lambda_{dem}$ (`r n.low.lam.at.max.nf` of `r n.stocks`) were found at the maximum abundance in the time series (Tables \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas) and \@ref(tab:tab-lamda-diffs) and Figures A1 and A2). However, two Atlantic cod stocks in the Northwest Atlantic had their lowest population growth rates observed at abundances markedly below the maximum. These Atlantic cod stocks seemed to have the least compensatory capacity at relative abundances near 40% of their maximum.  

There was generally an increase in the variability of the $\lambda$ estimates as abundance declined, largely due to the increase in the magnitude of the maximum value of $\lambda$ (Figure \@ref(fig:dd-overall-plt)). While there was a consistent overall pattern, the estimated random effects demonstrated substantial variability among stocks via the strength of negative density dependence. For example, stocks in the Western Atlantic (particularly Atlantic cod) and Alaska had some of the lowest $\lambda_{dem}$ estimates at low abundance, while several stocks in the North Sea (including Atlantic cod) had among the highest $\lambda_{dem}$ estimates  (Table \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas)).  Of the `r n.bl.40` stocks that declined below 40% of the maximum abundance, `r n.low.40.nf` had $\lambda_{dem}$ estimates < 1 at 40% of their maximum abundance; when the effects of fishing were included, `r n.low.40.fish` of the stocks had $\lambda_{real}$  below 1 (Table \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas)).

## Recovery Potential

When excluding fishing mortality, the overall median lifetime reproductive success (i.e., the number of female spawners per female spawner) was `r r0.med` (mean = `r r0.mn`; Figures \@ref(fig:r0-6-plt) and A3). When fishing mortality was accounted for, the median reproductive success dropped to `r r0.med.fish` (mean = `r r0.mn.fish`). This difference between the mean and median for stocks experiencing exploitation again highlighted the importance of occasional large reproductive events in sustaining these harvested stocks (Figures \@ref(fig:r0-6-plt) and A3). For species found across the North Atlantic, the lifetime reproductive success when excluding fishing mortality tended to be higher in the east than the west, which again was most evident in Atlantic cod (*G. morhua*) stocks. While the reproductive potential of cohorts within a stock could be highly variable, there were no clear temporal trends in lifetime reproductive success (Figures \@ref(fig:r0-nf-ts-plt) and \@ref(fig:r0-fish-ts-plt)).

Generation length (calculated as the mean age of spawners contributing to a recruit cohort) was lower and tended to be less variable under fishing across all stocks (Figures \@ref(fig:gl-6-plt) and \@ref(fig:gl-other-plt)). Similar to other metrics, there were regional and inter-specific patterns. For example, Atlantic herring (*C. harengus*) is typically considered to be a short-lived species yet its generation length in the Central and Western Atlantic tended to be higher than the generation length of Atlantic cod (*G. morhua*) and haddock (*M. aeglefinus*) in the Eastern Atlantic (Figure \@ref(fig:gl-6-plt)). Similar to lifetime reproductive output, there were no obvious temporal trends in the generation length among cohorts for the stocks in this analysis  (Figures \@ref(fig:gl-nf-ts-plt) and \@ref(fig:gl-fish-ts-plt)).

Based on simulated stock trajectories, the doubling time in the absence of fishing was relatively high for the majority of species (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-time-map)). Of the `r n.stocks` stocks in this analysis, `r n.dub.10` were classified with a high recovery potential which increased to `r n.stocks - n.not.dub.20` if those having a moderate recovery potential after 20 years were included (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-ts)). Unlike stocks with higher recovery potential,, there were clear regional patterns among stocks with low recovery potential. Of the `r n.not.dub.20` stocks in this analysis classified as having low recovery potential, `r n.alaska.slow` were in Alaska and `r n.nwa.slow` were in NAFO Regions 2-4 of the Western Atlantic. This meant that `r prop.slow.alaska`% and `r prop.slow.n24`% of assessed stocks in Alaska and NAFO Regions 2-4, respectively, were classified as having a low recovery potential. This contrasts to `r n.nea.slow` of the `r n.nea` stocks in the Eastern Atlantic classified with low recovery potential in the absence of fishing (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-time-map)).

Doubling time was influenced both by the magnitude and variability of $\lambda_{dem}$. Stocks with a median $\lambda_{dem} < 1$  were classified as having moderate to high recovery potential whenever the mean $\lambda_{dem}$ was $\gtrsim$ `r lam.rebuild.safe` or the standard deviation in $\lambda$ was $\gtrsim$ `r sd.rebuild.safe` (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-vs-sd)). In contrast, stocks with a median $\lambda_{dem}$ near 1 and with low variability tended to be classified as having low recovery potential.
